challenges.name: providers-di-quiz
challenges.title: Who creates the dependency?
challenges.description: Two versions of the CodeDev EnrollmentService wiring: one whose unit test still reached Postgres, and one that asks for a clock typed with an interface.

questions.explanation: True. Nest can only inject what a class asks for through its constructor. EnrollmentService has no constructor parameters, so Nest creates it with no arguments, and the field initializer runs new PgEnrollmentRepository(), which connects to Postgres. The provider { provide: PgEnrollmentRepository, useValue: fakeRepo } is registered, but nothing asks for that token, so it is never used. The fix is constructor(private readonly enrollments: EnrollmentRepository, private readonly clock: Clock) with abstract-class tokens; then the testing module (or a plain new EnrollmentService(fake, fixedClock)) decides what is injected, and the new Date() goes away too. The misconception is that registering a fake in the testing module replaces every use of the class: it replaces only what Nest injects.

False. Interfaces are erased when TypeScript compiles, so the constructor metadata records the parameter type as Object, and Nest matches parameters to providers by token, never by which methods a class has. Startup fails with: Nest can't resolve dependencies of the EnrollmentService (?). Please make sure that the argument Object at index [0] is available in the EnrollmentModule context. The fix is a token that exists at runtime: make Clock an abstract class and register { provide: Clock, useClass: SystemClock }, or keep the interface and use a symbol token, { provide: CLOCK, useClass: SystemClock } with @Inject(CLOCK) on the parameter. The misconception is that Nest wires dependencies by structural typing, the way the TypeScript compiler checks them.

challenges.name: enrollment-service-injected-clock
challenges.title: Inject the repository and the clock
challenges.description: CodeDev premium access lasts 30 days from the moment a learner enrolls. The old EnrollmentService created its own PgEnrollmentRepository and read the time with new Date(), so it could only be tested against Postgres and failed near midnight. Write EnrollmentService with constructor(repo: EnrollmentRepository, clock: Clock): keep both and use them for everything. Never create a repository and never read the current time with new Date() or Date.now(): the time is clock.now() (new Date(milliseconds) to build a date is fine). Read enrollments from repo on every call, because an admin tool can change the repository between calls. enroll(userId, courseId): throw an Error and save nothing when userId or courseId is empty or only spaces; when the learner already has access, return that enrollment unchanged and save nothing; otherwise (no enrollment, or an expired one) save and return { userId, courseId, enrolledAt: now, expiresAt: now + ACCESS_DAYS (30) days }, both as toISOString() strings. hasAccess(userId, courseId): true when the repository has an enrollment for the pair and now is before expiresAt (at exactly expiresAt, access has ended). daysLeft(userId, courseId): 0 without access, otherwise the time until expiresAt in days rounded up (30 right after enrolling, still 30 one hour later, 1 when less than a day is left). The test runner reads { now, existing, operations } as JSON, builds the service with an in-memory repository holding the existing enrollments and a fixed clock that starts at now and moves only on { op: "advance", hours }, runs enroll, hasAccess, daysLeft and revoke (the admin tool deletes from the repository) in order, and prints one line per call plus the number of save() calls.
hints: In each of your three methods, where does the current time come from, and where does the enrollment come from? If either answer is not "from something the constructor received", how could a test running at 10 a.m. check what happens at midnight, or see an enrollment it put into the repository?

Start with the constructor: a parameter property such as private readonly repo: EnrollmentRepository stores the argument as a field in one line. Then in every method call this.repo.findOne(userId, courseId) rather than remembering enrollments yourself, compare this.clock.now().getTime() with Date.parse(expiresAt), and decide what both methods return at exactly expiresAt. daysLeft rounds up, so think about Math.ceil and Math.floor.

A similar service on other data: a CouponService(repo, clock) where a coupon is valid for 7 days. Created at 2026-03-01T10:00:00.000Z, its validUntil is new Date(created.getTime() + 7 * DAY_MS).toISOString() = 2026-03-08T10:00:00.000Z. With a clock at 2026-03-07T12:00:00.000Z, 22 hours are left, so the days left are Math.ceil(22 / 24) = 1; with the clock at exactly 2026-03-08T10:00:00.000Z the coupon is no longer valid and 0 days are left. A test builds it as new CouponService(new InMemoryCouponRepository(), { now: () => new Date("2026-03-07T12:00:00.000Z") }).

tests.name: Enroll at 23:59: 30 days of access, still 30 days left one hour later, after midnight
An enrollment already in the repository: read it, and enrolling again saves nothing
Access ends exactly at expiresAt; enrolling after that starts a new 30 days
Partial days round up: 23 hours left is 1 day, 25 hours left is 2 days
Revoked in the repository by an admin tool: no access, and enrolling starts fresh
A blank user or course id is rejected and nothing is saved
Large: 60 existing enrollments, 120 learners and 800 operations while the clock moves on
